We break down what makes SCHD’s methodology unique, how the ETF has consistently grown its dividend, and whether someone could safely retire with a portfolio consisting entirely of SCHD.

We also discuss:

Why Craig started investing in SCHD
His plan to build a $1 million SCHD position by 2035
The two primary drivers of SCHD’s dividend growth
Whether SCHD provides enough diversification for retirement
How SCHD can reduce sequence-of-returns risk
Whether option-income ETFs should be paired with SCHD
Craig’s thoughts on OVL, GPIQ, GPIX, SPYI and QQQI
Whether SCHD can continue outperforming in 2026 and beyond
Craig’s dividend-growth estimate for 2026
Why Craig believes Meta stock may currently be mispriced

Schwab isn't trying to time anything.   The stocks are selected yearly,  then quarterly rebalanced to make sure they fit the chosen guidelines.   THEY ARE NOT PICKING STOCKS BECAUSE THEY "LIKE' THEM.  An example of quarterly reblancing would be---- lets say Coke is doing so well price wise that it represents more than 4% of SHED.   There guidlines say no one stock should ever be more than 4% of the portfolio, so they would sell some Coke  to get it down to below 4% of portfolio.       Let's say the funds drug or health care stocks grown in value to over 25% of a sector.   They would cut back health care stocks because there rule is no more than 25% of any sector.   Then they would take this money and simply buy stock types that are already there to rebalance.       Sequence of return concerns when you are forced to sell stock to raise cash-   this kills the goose that lays the golden egg.

What's great about SCHD is the methodology that they use to add stocks to their list of holdings, I would say it's probably close to being unique in dividend ETF funds. Removing lower yielding stocks and replacing them with higher yielding ones is just part of the story, because it just so happens that many of these higher yielding stocks are companies whose share prices have declined to the point of them being underpriced (stock price goes down, yield goes up), and the fund managers feel that the share price has room to grow based on the financials of the company. So not only do you get good current dividend yields, but dividends that have a history of growing, AND share prices of the companies that have the potential to go up rather than staying stagnant. You get the best of both worlds with SCHD.

If you are simply reinvesting the dividend (DRIP) and are a long term investor, why should anyone invest in SCHD? I can understand if you need the income and are spending the dividends (but that means NO DRIP). Investors that are young and thus their time horizon is long term, should invest in growth and concentrate on total return. I see too many youtubers and people that are young emphasizing dividend (and dividend growth) stocks or ETFs/mutual funds (like SCHD). Their justification is to build a portfolio of income/dividend producing stocks or ETFs/mutual funds. However, if they are simply reinvesting that income/dividends, it would be more advantageous to get a better overall total return. Then later on in life transform their portfolio to stocks that produce income/dividends. Too much emphasis on high yield dividend stocks/ETFs/mutual funds at a young age will ultimately result in less overall wealth in the future. If you take a look at a time frame of SCHD's inception to now (as of 08/21/2026), here are their total returns (dividends reinvestment included) for a $10,000 investment:

The numbers, obviously, show that over that time period (since the inception of SCHD), all of these other ETFs/mutual funds are much better choices. But if you are a long term investor, ignore the volatility and just hold an investment that will give a superior total return over the long term.
